Read all three files first, then make these edits:

## Edit 1: Fix 22× claim [CRITICAL]
In introduction.tex, contribution (2), change "type identity explaining 22$\times$ more variance than model identity" → "clause identity explaining 22$\times$ more variance than model identity". The 22× ratio is clause identity (22.4%) vs model (1.0%), NOT type identity vs model. Type only explains 0.4%.

## Edit 2: Demote C4 from Introduction [MUST-FIX]
In introduction.tex, the overview paragraph (starts "Our results show that all policy ambiguity is nocuous..."), reduce C4/auth_scope prominence. Currently it devotes a full sentence to "authorization scope shows the widest cross-model range (52\,pp)..." with κ caveat. 

Replace the current text from "but that type primarily determines severity, with a smaller but significant model$\times$type interaction (2.9\% of variance). Incompleteness is consistently high (46--62\% violation rate across all models), while authorization scope shows the widest cross-model range (52\,pp), though this is an upper bound with substantial measurement uncertainty ($\kappa = 0.385$, below fair agreement; \S Limitations), suggesting that safety training may differentially mitigate specific ambiguity types." with something like: "with type primarily determining severity. Incompleteness is consistently high (46--62\% across all models); an exploratory model$\times$type interaction (\S\ref{sec:c4}) suggests differential vulnerability across type--model combinations."

This removes the 52pp specific number and the κ detail from the intro body, demoting C4 to a brief mention pointing to the section.

## Edit 3: Hedge "first causal quantification" [BONUS]
In introduction.tex, contribution (1), change "the first causal quantification of policy ambiguity's safety impact via matched-pair design with perturbation control" → "the first matched-pair causal study of policy ambiguity's safety impact with perturbation control"

## Edit 4: DN novelty hedging [SHOULD-FIX]
In introduction.tex, contribution (3), add a parenthetical citing prior work to show DN builds on known phenomena. Currently: "an error analysis revealing \emph{Disambiguation Neglect} ($\leq$11\% awareness) and \emph{systematic nocuity}---41.3\% of ambiguous clauses trigger majority-convergent violations, indicating clause-level risk factors"

Change to something like: "an error analysis revealing \emph{Disambiguation Neglect}---extending LLM ambiguity-collapse findings \citep{liu_ambiguity_2023,hu_ambiguity_2025} to agentic settings---with $\leq$11\% awareness, and \emph{systematic nocuity}: 41.3\% of ambiguous clauses trigger majority-convergent violations, indicating clause-level risk factors"

The key point: DN is not claiming a completely novel phenomenon. It extends prior findings about LLM single-output collapse to the safety-relevant agentic context.

## Verification
After edits, verify:
- abstract.tex needs NO changes (already has "risk gradient", no 22× or 52pp, DN phrasing is fine)
- conclusion.tex needs NO changes (already says "clause identity", no 52pp, no two-tier)
- introduction.tex has all 4 edits applied correctly
- No LaTeX syntax errors introduced

1	\section{Introduction}
2	\label{sec:introduction}
3	
4	A customer asks to return a customized item within the 30-day window. The agent consults the store policy, which states that ``items may be returned within 30 days.'' The word ``items'' scopes over all product categories, including custom orders that are normally final sale. The agent grants a full refund and arranges free return shipping. One word of scopal ambiguity costs the retailer \$200.
5	
6	LLM-based agents increasingly operate under natural-language policy specifications that govern their permitted actions. These specifications inevitably contain ambiguity: a property that has been studied for decades in requirements engineering (RE) and computational linguistics. \citet{berry_kamsties_2004} distinguish between \emph{nocuous} (i.e., harmful) ambiguity, where different stakeholders arrive at different interpretations, and \emph{innocuous} ambiguity, where shared organizational context ensures convergent interpretation. In human RE workflows, most ambiguity is innocuous because developers share domain knowledge, can consult colleagues, and iteratively clarify requirements.
7	
8	LLM agents lack these disambiguation channels. They cannot consult colleagues, rarely escalate to users, and must resolve ambiguity in real time from the text alone. This raises a question that has not been empirically addressed: does policy ambiguity cause safety violations in LLM agents, and if so, does the \emph{type} of ambiguity predict the severity of the violation? Prior work classifies ambiguity types in policies \citep{drip_r_2026,li_ambiguity_taxonomy_2024} or measures policy understanding quality \citep{policybank_2026}, but no existing study provides a causal, type-granularity mapping from ambiguity to safety violations.
9	
10	\begin{figure*}[t]
11	\centering
12	\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures/fig1_overview.pdf}
13	\caption{Experimental overview. We construct 300 matched clause pairs across a six-type, two-layer ambiguity taxonomy and inject them into $\tau^2$-bench policy documents. Five models interact with the modified policies across 2,997 episodes. A cross-judge evaluation pipeline classifies violation severity on a four-tier scale.}
14	\label{fig:overview}
15	\end{figure*}
16	
17	We address this gap with a matched-pair causal study on $\tau^2$-bench \citep{tau2_bench_2025}, a dual-control conversational agent benchmark. Using a six-type taxonomy organized into two layers (linguistic and specification, \S\ref{sec:taxonomy}), we construct 300 ambiguous/unambiguous clause pairs and evaluate five architecturally diverse models across 2,997 episodes.
18	
19	Our results show that all policy ambiguity is nocuous for LLM agents ($+34.0$ pp violation rate increase, OR $= 15.1$), but that type primarily determines severity, with a smaller but significant model$\times$type interaction (2.9\% of variance). Incompleteness is consistently high (46--62\% violation rate across all models), while authorization scope shows the widest cross-model range (52\,pp), though this is an upper bound with substantial measurement uncertainty ($\kappa = 0.385$, below fair agreement; \S Limitations), suggesting that safety training may differentially mitigate specific ambiguity types. Agents exhibit disambiguation neglect in over 89\% of cases, with fewer than 11\% showing any disambiguation awareness.
20	
21	Our contributions are: (1)~the first causal quantification of policy ambiguity's safety impact via matched-pair design with perturbation control (\S\ref{sec:method}), observed across five primary models and confirmed in two additional replication models; (2)~incompleteness as a consistent upper-bound risk type across all models and margins, with type identity explaining 22$\times$ more variance than model identity (\S\ref{sec:results}); and (3)~an error analysis revealing \emph{Disambiguation Neglect} ($\leq$11\% awareness) and \emph{systematic nocuity}---41.3\% of ambiguous clauses trigger majority-convergent violations, indicating clause-level risk factors (\S\ref{sec:analysis}).
22

1	\section{Conclusion}
2	
3	Ambiguous policy clauses increase agent safety violations by 34.0\,pp (OR\,$=$\,15.1) across five models, with clause identity explaining 22$\times$ more variance than model identity. Incompleteness consistently ranks highest across all seven models ($\geq$46\%), with rankings replicating in independent families ($\rho = 0.60$--$0.90$). With agents exhibiting disambiguation neglect in over 89\% of cases and 41.3\% of clauses triggering model-convergent violations, type-aware auditing and externalized detection are critical for policy-governed deployments.
4
